Something is compulsory when you must do it — not because you want to, but because a law, rule, or authority requires you to. You have no real choice. If you don't do it, there will be consequences.

Think of it this way: the opposite of compulsory is optional. If something is optional, you can choose. If something is compulsory, you cannot.
The Core Idea: Where Does the Force Come From?

The key thing to understand about "compulsory" is that the force comes from outside you — from a government, an institution, a rule, or an authority. It's not your own desire or inner need. Someone or something above you has decided that this thing must happen, and you don't get a vote.

This is important because it separates "compulsory" from words like "necessary." Something can be necessary based on logic or your own goals ("sleep is necessary for health"). But something compulsory is demanded by an external authority — it's enforced, not just advised.

Compulsory is a strong word. It doesn't mean "strongly encouraged" or "expected." It means legally or formally required — and often, failing to comply carries a real penalty. A fine. A legal punishment. Expulsion. Disqualification. Something official happens if you refuse or ignore it.

So on a scale of obligation:

  • Suggested → mild
  • Expected → moderate
  • Required → strong
  • Compulsory → very strong (backed by rules or law, enforced)

1. Compulsory education
In most countries, children must go to school until a certain age. They don't have a say. Their parents don't have a say. The law demands it. That's compulsory education.

2. Compulsory military service
In some countries, every citizen (often every young man) must serve in the military for a period of time. Even if they don't want to, they have no legal choice. This is called compulsory military service.

3. Compulsory voting
In countries like Australia, every eligible citizen is legally required to vote in elections. Not voting results in a fine.

4. Compulsory insurance
In many places, if you own and drive a car, you are legally required to have car insurance. You cannot legally drive without it. It is compulsory.

5. Compulsory retirement
Some organizations or laws force employees to retire at a certain age, regardless of whether they want to continue working.

6. Compulsory subjects in school
Even within a school, some subjects — like mathematics or a national language — are compulsory. Every student must study them. Other subjects may be elective (chosen freely). Compulsory subjects are not.

• "Wearing a seatbelt is compulsory in most countries."
  • "Attendance at the safety training is compulsory for all new employees."
  • "The government announced compulsory vaccination for healthcare workers."
  • "History is a compulsory subject in our school; you cannot skip it."
  • "The military draft made service compulsory for men between the ages of 18 and 25."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Compulsory vs. Mandatory
These two words are nearly identical in meaning and are often interchangeable. Both mean "required by a rule or law." Mandatory is slightly more common in formal legal and corporate settings, while compulsory is used more in everyday language, especially in education and government policy. In practice, you can usually use either one.

Compulsory vs. Obligatory
Obligatory also means required, but it can sometimes carry a sense of moral or social duty, not just legal or formal duty. "Saying thank you is obligatory in polite society" — not a law, but a social expectation. Compulsory, on the other hand, almost always implies a formal rule or law with real enforcement.

Compulsory vs. Required
Required is a softer, more neutral word. It simply means "needed" or "asked for." Compulsory is stronger — it implies that the requirement is formal, official, and comes with enforcement. All compulsory things are required, but not all required things are compulsory.

Compulsory vs. Forced
Forced suggests more direct pressure or coercion — often physical or psychological. "He was forced to sign the contract." Compulsory is more impersonal and systemic — it's a rule of the system, not someone physically making you do something.

Compulsory vs. Involuntary
Involuntary means something that happens without your will or without your control — sometimes even unconsciously (an involuntary reflex). Compulsory is specifically about being required to do something — you're still performing the action, but you have no legal or institutional choice.

If something is compulsory, its opposite is:

  • Optional — you can choose to do it or not
  • Voluntary — you do it willingly, of your own free choice
  • Elective — you select it yourself (often used in education: elective courses vs. compulsory courses)
  • Discretionary — left to someone's own judgment or choice

These are the most natural combinations in which "compulsory" appears:

  • Compulsory education — schooling required by law for children
  • Compulsory military service — legally required time in the armed forces
  • Compulsory attendance — you must be present
  • Compulsory purchase — a legal power allowing a government to force someone to sell their property (common in British English)
  • Compulsory redundancy — when an employer is forced by circumstances to dismiss workers (British English, used in employment law)
  • Compulsory retirement — forced retirement at a fixed age
  • Compulsory voting — legally required participation in elections
  • Compulsory insurance — insurance that the law requires you to have
  • Compulsory measures — actions that must be taken under a rule or law
  • Make something compulsory — to pass a rule requiring something

"Compulsory" is a neutral to formal word. It's not rude, emotional, or casual. You'll find it in newspapers, laws, school policies, government documents, and formal writing. It's perfectly natural in everyday speech too — "Is this session compulsory?" is something a student might ask a teacher quite naturally.

It doesn't carry a negative or positive emotional charge on its own. Whether the compulsory thing is good or bad depends entirely on context. Compulsory education is widely seen as a positive thing. Compulsory military service might be seen positively or negatively depending on who you ask. The word itself is simply descriptive.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Compulsory = you must do it, because a rule or authority demands it, and you have no real choice.
